column1: Data without geography is a map without territory
column2: Every dataset must be anchored to extraction/concentration/displacement zones. A CO2 reading is meaningless without knowing who emitted and who breathes.

column1: Data without time is a snapshot without story
column2: Every dataset must carry temporal depth. A soil test is a single frame; a 30-year SOC trend is a narrative of care or neglect.
Anavaratha cares more about whether things are getting better or worse (direction) than about precise numbers. Qualitative trend is sufficient.

column1: The most important data is the hardest to find
column2: Olfactory, sound baselines, cultural reservoir health, attentional ecology—these are the domains where data poverty is highest and where collapse is most invisible.
When direct measurement doesn't exist, creative proxies must be constructed. Literary descriptions of soundscapes. Street View images for visual clutter. Respiratory illness for olfactory burden.

column1: Citizen science is not backup—it's primary
column2: For sensory ecologies especially, distributed human observers are the best (sometimes only) sensors. eBird, iNaturalist, SmellPittsburgh—these are paradigmatic.

column1: Displacement zones need monitoring most, have it least
column2: Deliberate counter-investment: Anavaratha prioritizes data from where costs land, not where profits accumulate.
Track the condition of wetlands, soil carbon, silence zones, language vitality BEFORE tracking visible damage. Reservoir erosion IS the early warning.
The final insight layer requires combining across ecologies: a place where air is polluted AND noisy AND visually cluttered AND losing its language = total negentropic collapse.
A gap in the map is information. Where data doesn't exist, the absence itself reveals something about what society has chosen not to see.
